newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: APEC promise a tease for Manila's exotic dancers.
newsitem.headline: APEC promise a tease for Manila's exotic dancers.

text.p: To Bill Clinton and other Asia-Pacific leaders, APEC means business but to Kim Padilla and hundreds of other striptease dancers in Manila's nightclub row, APEC is no business at all.
Wild Duck should have been a full house on a weekend night.
But the place was barely half filled and Kim and a dozen other dancers were twiddling their thumbs wondering when their regular customers would show up and buy drinks.
"I am not happy with APEC. Before, we had a lot of customers, all the girls have customers, but now over half of the girls don't have customers," the 20-year old said.
"No customer, no income."

Before APEC politicians and officials descended on the city to plot the region's future prosperity, Kim would have had a poor night if she had gone home with less than 2,000 pesos ($75) in her wallet from drink commissions and tips.
Now, she said, she would be lucky if she earned half of that.

Owners, dancers and waiters in the dozens of glittering night clubs, bars and restaurants on seaside Roxas Boulevard had thought business would boom when the Philippines hosted the summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum. That's what all the politicians had said.
After all, an estimated 6,500 officials, businessmen and media people from 18 economies responsible for more than half of the world's economic output were coming to town.
Many would be living and holding meetings in glittering buildings and five star hotels -- symbols of booming Asia -- on the same boulevard where Kim works.
Some clubowners spruced up their places to make a good impression. One dreamed up a special attraction just for the APEC folks -- it imported prostitutes from a former Russian republic.
At least one club strung up a "Welcome APEC delegates" streamer and flags of APEC members that were bigger than most of the girls' costumes.
None of it worked.
On any given night, floor manager Aida Badeo said, the Vagabond would have about 100 customers. This night, there were fewer than 50.
And, like the customers at Wild Duck, none of the foreigners looked like they had anything at all to do with APEC. One sported spectacular tatoos on his biceps.

Wild Duck owner Danny Espiritu blamed the sudden recession on tight police security, which included setting up mobile checkpoints, and the designation of so-called "APEC Friendship Lanes" on Manila's notoriously clogged highways.
Officials supervising the capital's chaotic traffic reserved the lanes for vehicles bearing special APEC stickers to allow delegates to swish around town with the greatest of ease.
The lanes delighted the visitors but drew curses from ordinary mortals caught in monumental traffic jams as they were crammed into the remaining lanes.
A government ban on the carrying of even licensed guns in public places, part of APEC special security, also probably persuaded some pleasure-seekers to stay at home.
Many Filipinos drive around with guns hidden in their vehicles as protection against criminals.
"Most of my clientele and foreign guests would rather stay home than go out because of all this security," Espiritu said.
